title: Family How a Christian Man Dies McGrew, Beth
author: McGrew, Beth
summary: Beth McGrew uses a scene from Netflix's Inside the Manosphere documentary as a launching point for a reflection on what it means for a man to die well as a Christian, set against the manosphere's philosophy that 'men aren't supposed to be happy.' She traces the emergence of 'looksmaxxing' and similar practices -- grotesque self-improvement regimens premised on the idea that masculinity is primarily expressed through endurance of pain -- and argues they represent a distorted secular theology of suffering. McGrew contrasts this with the Christian theology of the cross, which acknowledges real suffering but situates it within a narrative of redemption, love, and ultimate hope rather than stoic endurance for its own sake. The article draws on historical examples of Christian men who died well to articulate what the manosphere gets right about masculine virtue and catastrophically wrong about its meaning.
points: The manosphere's 'men aren't supposed to be happy' philosophy contains a true insight -- that a life of meaning requires endurance of difficulty -- but distorts it by severing suffering from love, redemption, and hope, leaving only grim performance of pain without the context that makes suffering worthwhile.

Looksmaxxing and similar self-harm regimens reflect an accurate perception that men need challenge and discipline applied to an entirely wrong object -- suffering for its own sake in service of vanity rather than for genuine goods.

Christian theology has a richer account of masculine suffering than the manosphere: the cross represents not stoic endurance but sacrificial love -- suffering entered voluntarily not to display toughness but to protect and redeem others.

Historical Christian martyrs and deathbed witnesses died with attention directed outward -- toward God, toward those they loved, toward hope -- rather than inward toward their own performance of fortitude, which is the structural difference between Christian dying and manosphere stoicism.

Young men who find the manosphere's philosophy compelling are responding to a genuine need for a meaningful account of masculine difficulty, and the church's failure to offer a compelling alternative is partly responsible for the vacuum the manosphere fills.
quotes: In Netflix's documentary Inside the Manosphere, there is a wrenching scene between mild-mannered host Louis Theroux and two fanboys of Justin Waller, one of the odious streamers Theroux has set out (with mixed success) to deflate. Unlike their idol, these young men come across as nice lads, albeit hopelessly lost. One of them reveals that he first moved to Miami to try to "make it big" when he was wrestling with grief over his brother's suicide.
